Bootstrapped business: Precision Aesthetics Lab

[ops][assistant] To get us started, could you describe in plain language what "Precision Aesthetics Lab" does or will do—what you sell or deliver, and how you expect to get paid for it (if it's easier, you can start with something simple like "fitness gym", "law firm", "restaurant", etc.)?
[user] Precision Aesthetics Lab provides advanced non-surgical aesthetic treatments with a focus on high-ticket procedures delivered in a clinical studio setting. Clients primarily book and pay for individual treatment sessions online or through paid advertising channels.

[ops][assistant] Here’s how I’m understanding Precision Aesthetics Lab: it’s an in-person clinical aesthetics studio that delivers advanced, non-surgical cosmetic treatments as individual treatment sessions, with clients typically booking and paying per session rather than through memberships or subscriptions. Value is delivered through one-off, appointment-based procedures performed in the studio, and most revenue comes from these single-session, high-ticket treatments that clients book online after finding you via your website or paid ads. For operations and revenue, we’ll treat the core unit as one treatment session on a weekly cadence (how many sessions can be delivered per week).

Is this description accurate as the main way the business works?
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] Based on the start date you provided, I'm treating this as operating for planning context. If that's off, tell me and I'll adjust.

Next, who are you primarily selling these treatment sessions to—individual consumers, other businesses (like clinics/med spas), or a meaningful mix of both?
[user] Primarily individual consumers.

[ops][assistant] Got it—primarily individual consumers.

Next, for a typical full week when you’re “fully booked” at your current or near-term staffing and room setup, about how many individual treatment sessions could you realistically perform in the studio in that week (not what you hope for long-term, but what’s achievable with your current setup)?
[user] At full capacity, I can handle up to 55 treatment sessions per week.

[ops][assistant] 55 sessions per week at full capacity makes sense for a high-ticket, appointment-based studio.

For planning, I’d suggest we assume you’ll realistically run at about 70–80% of that practical capacity in Year 1 (to allow for no-shows, admin time, slower weeks, etc.). Does using 75% of capacity for Year 1 sound about right, or would you prefer a different rough percentage?
[user] I prefer to use 88% utilization for Year 1 instead of 75%.

[ops][assistant] Just to confirm, what should we record for milestones' Please give a single number or short value.
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] Perfect, we’ll use 88% of your practical weekly capacity for Year 1.

Next, let’s lock in pricing for your main unit: for one high-ticket aesthetic treatment session (a single in-person procedure appointment), what is the average price you plan to charge per session across your typical mix of treatments?
[user] The average price per treatment session will be $875.

[ops][assistant] Thanks, we’ll use $875 as the average price per high-ticket treatment session.

To confirm how clients actually receive the service: my assumption is that every treatment is delivered in person at your clinical studio in Dallas as a scheduled appointment (no mobile/at-home visits, no telehealth component). Is that accurate?
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] Thanks, that matches what I had.

For sales channels, would you say clients mainly book and pay through in-person visits, online (website/booking platform), or is it a fairly even hybrid of both?
[user] Clients primarily book through paid ads and online scheduling.

[ops][assistant] Got it, so your main sales and booking flow is online via paid ads driving people into your online scheduling/booking system.

For geography, are you aiming to serve mainly the local Dallas area (people coming into the Dallas studio), or do you think of your reach as more regional across Texas, national, or broader?
[user] Mostly local Dallas metro area clients with some traveling from surrounding regions.

[ops][assistant] Given that most clients are coming into your Dallas studio, I’d frame your service area as local to the Dallas–Fort Worth metro and nearby North Texas communities. Does “Dallas–Fort Worth metro area and surrounding North Texas cities” sound like the right way to describe your main service area?
[user] Yes, Dallas metro area with some clients traveling from surrounding regions is the best way to describe it.

[ops][assistant] Understood, we’ll describe your main service area as the Dallas metro area with some clients traveling in from surrounding regions.

Next, for your legal structure, which label fits Precision Aesthetics Lab best right now: Sole proprietor, LLC, LLP, S-corp, C-corp, or Partnership?
[user] LLC.

[ops][assistant] Thanks, we’ll record Precision Aesthetics Lab as an LLC.

One more structural item: thinking about what limits how many treatment sessions you can deliver in a week, is the main constraint your own/clinical staff time and room availability (labor), your systems/technology and booking flow (system), or simply having enough client demand (demand)?
[user] The main constraint is labor—my own clinical time and room availability limit how many sessions I can deliver each week.

[ops][assistant] Proposed competitive advantage: Your core competitive advantage is a deliberately narrow, high-skill procedure mix executed by a single lead clinician, which allows you to standardize protocols, tightly control outcomes, and maintain near-full utilization at a high price point. That advantage exists because you’ve chosen to run one high-ticket, appointment-based treatment line in a single studio, with capacity constrained by expert labor rather than multiple injectors or add-on services, so every operational choice (scheduling, equipment, training, marketing) is optimized around that one pattern of work. For patients, this translates into more consistent, predictable results and fewer failed or “redo” procedures, and it’s hard for competitors to copy without unwinding their broader menus, multi-provider staffing models, and volume-driven incentives.

Does this accurately reflect what truly sets the business apart?
[user] Yes, that description accurately captures the essence of what sets Precision Aesthetics Lab apart—our focused expertise and tight operational control to maximize the quality and consistency of every session.

[ops][assistant] Looking ahead, what is one concrete goal you want to hit in about the next 12 months (for example: a target number of weekly units/orders, a customer count, or a rough monthly revenue level)?
[user] My goal is to reach about 70 treatment sessions per week within 12 months.

[market][assistant] Great, let's move on to Target Market.

For your high-ticket aesthetic treatment sessions, do you want to focus mainly on women, mainly on men, or serve both genders without a strong skew?
[user] Mostly female but open to all.

[market][assistant] We’ll treat your core focus as primarily female clients, while still being open to all genders.

Next, what age range are you mainly aiming for with these high-ticket aesthetic treatments (for example, mid-20s to late 40s, 30–60, etc.)?
[user] I'm targeting adults aged 30 to 65 for the treatments.

[market][assistant] Great, we’ll center on adults roughly 30 to 65.

Given your price point per treatment session and that you’re a high-ticket, elective aesthetics studio, what annual household income range best fits your ideal clients (for example, $75k–$150k, $150k–$300k, or no real income preference as long as they can afford treatment)?
[user] The ideal clients typically have a household income of $60,000 and above to comfortably afford the treatments.

[market][assistant] Got it—household income of about $60,000 and above as your ideal floor makes sense for a high-ticket, elective service like this.

Next, thinking about education level, are you targeting any particular band, or is it fairly open as long as they value aesthetics and can afford treatment? For example:
- Mostly college-educated and above (bachelor’s, graduate, professional)
- Broad mix: high school and some college up through graduate degrees, no strong preference?
What feels most accurate for your ideal Dallas clients?
[user] It's a broad mix of education levels. We don't have a strict preference, as long as clients value aesthetics and can afford the treatments.

[market][assistant] That broad mix on education fits well with your offer and price point.

Given what you’re doing—a high-ticket, in-person aesthetics studio in the Dallas area—extra nuance about household structure, employment, and housing costs could help with messaging and pricing psychology, but it’s not strictly required.

Which, if any, of these would you like to dial in a bit more: household structure, employment, housing economics, any combination of those, or skip all three and keep it simple?
[user] Let's skip the household structure and housing economics details for now and just focus a bit more on employment. The target market is a mix of professionals and service workers, reflecting the diverse working population in Dallas.

[market][assistant] Great, a mix of professionals and service workers in the Dallas area makes sense for your price point and studio location.

To keep this simple and usable: would you say your employment focus is mainly on full-time workers (both salaried professionals and full-time service workers), or are part-time and gig workers equally core to your ideal client profile?
[user] My target market is indeed a mix of professionals and service workers; both full-time and part-time workers are included but the key segment is the mix you mentioned.

[market][assistant] Precision Aesthetics Lab will be positioned as a premium, local clinical aesthetics studio offering advanced non-surgical cosmetic procedures on a per-treatment session basis at approximately $875 per treatment session, designed for appearance-conscious women aged 30 to 65 in the Dallas metro area with household incomes of roughly $60,000 and above. Operating as an in-person, high-ticket practice constrained primarily by expert labor and treatment room availability, the studio will speak directly to a mix of professionals and service workers who seek consistent, medically grounded aesthetic outcomes and are willing to book and travel for focused, one-session-at-a-time treatments rather than memberships or volume deals, reinforcing its role as a specialized, outcomes-driven destination rather than a generic med spa.

To acquire these clients efficiently at scale, the marketing architecture will center on five priority channels: Google Search to capture high-intent local prospects actively looking for specific aesthetic procedures and willing to pay premium prices; Google Maps/Business Profile to convert nearby searchers who value proximity, reviews, and clinical credibility when choosing a local provider; Instagram to visually showcase before-and-after results and reinforce the studio’s advanced, clinical aesthetic positioning for women in the 30–65 age band; Facebook to reach a broader mix of local professionals and service workers with interest-based and demographic targeting aligned to your income and age profile; and referral partnerships with complementary local professionals (such as salons, personal trainers, and wellness providers) whose clientele overlaps with your target demographic and is predisposed to invest in appearance-related services. This narrative defines the strategic marketing architecture and will be expanded into a detailed execution-level marketing plan in the full written business plan.

Does this look right before we move on to Human Resources?
[user] Yes, that summary looks right to me. I'm happy with this marketing positioning and strategy. Let's move on to Human Resources.

[people][assistant] Great, let's move on to Human Resources.

For Precision Aesthetics Lab, most businesses at your operating stage usually highlight just a few pivotal roles (leadership, clinical/licensed, operations, and key client-facing people), simply to show the real capacity that exists today.

Let’s start with the primary clinical/lead role:  
What is this person’s full name, current title/role in the business, total years of relevant experience in aesthetics/medicine (number of years), and any relevant education or credentials (degrees, licenses, certifications)?
[user] The founder is a licensed nurse practitioner with 6 years of experience in aesthetics.

[people][assistant] Thanks, that’s helpful. To capture this person properly, could you share their:

- Full name  
- Current title/role in Precision Aesthetics Lab (for example, Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner)  
- Total years of relevant experience (we’ll note 6 in aesthetics; add any prior relevant clinical experience if you want it counted)  
- Key education and credentials (degrees, licenses, and notable certifications)

Once we’ve got that person, we’ll see if you want to add anyone else.

Understood. For this founder/lead clinician, what is their full name?
[user] Her name is Emily Carter. She is the Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner with 6 years of experience in aesthetics. She holds a Master of Science in Nursing and is a licensed nurse practitioner with certifications in advanced aesthetic procedures.

[people][assistant] Got it on Emily Carter as Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner with her background and credentials.

Would you like to add another person who is important to how Precision Aesthetics Lab operates today (for example, another clinician, an operations/office manager, or a marketing/administrative lead)?
[user] No, there are no additional staff members at launch.

[people][assistant] Review this draft (key people narrative + suggested year-1 roles with wages and timing) and tell me any changes.

Emily Carter serves as Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner, bringing a Master of Science in Nursing, nurse practitioner licensure, and certifications in advanced aesthetic procedures, backed by 6 years of focused experience in aesthetic medicine. She personally delivers all high-ticket, non-surgical treatments, designs and enforces clinical protocols, and oversees safety, compliance, and patient experience, which ensures that Precision Aesthetics Lab can execute a narrow, high-skill procedure mix at a consistently high standard. By combining hands-on clinical expertise with direct operational leadership, she anchors the studio’s ability to maintain predictable outcomes, protect against quality lapses, and sustain near-full utilization of the treatment schedule as demand grows. Estimated annual wage: $135,460/year.

Suggested year-1 roles and estimated annual wages:
- Patient Coordinator & Front Desk Lead: $46,740/year (in ~0 months) - Needed immediately to handle check-in, scheduling, payment processing, and basic patient communication so clinical time stays focused on revenue-generating treatments.
- Medical Assistant / Aesthetic Clinical Assistant: $48,350/year (in ~6 months) - Becomes important as weekly volume approaches the upper end of capacity to support room turnover, prep, and post-care so the lead clinician can maximize treatment time.
- Digital Marketing & Patient Acquisition Specialist (Part-Time or Contractor): $85,420/year (in ~3 months) - Needed within the first few months to manage paid ads, tracking, and campaign optimization to consistently fill the schedule at the planned price point.
- Practice Manager (Part-Time, evolving to Full-Time): $130,140/year (in ~9 months) - Becomes valuable once the practice is running at high utilization to own operations, vendor management, and basic finance/admin so the founder is less of a bottleneck.

Does this look right before we move on to Financials?
[user] Yes, that looks right.

[financials][assistant] Great, let's move on to Financials.

Year 1 revenue:

| Line of Business | Product / Unit | Capacity | Load / Utilization | Price | Periods / Year | Year-1 Revenue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primary line of business | High-ticket aesthetic treatment session | 55 treatment session/week | 88% | $875 | 52 | $2,202,200 |
| **Primary line of business total** |  |  |  |  |  | **$2,202,200** |
| **Company Total** |  |  |  |  |  | **$2,202,200** |

This planning baseline assumes you run at about 88% utilization of 55 sessions per week, at an average price of $875, across 52 operating periods, which produces about $2,202,200 in Year-1 revenue. We will use this as the baseline for the rest of financial planning.
[user] Yes, that's right.

[financials][assistant] Got it — we’ll use $2,202,200 as your Year-1 revenue baseline for the rest of the financial planning.

A reasonable Year-1 COGS baseline is about 57% of revenue, which puts your projected Year-1 direct costs around $1,260,022.

Does that broadly match how your business works, or should we adjust it because your direct costs are materially different?
[user] Actually, our direct costs are much lower. We plan to use 22% COGS based on our operational estimates for Year 1.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll set your Year-1 direct costs to 22% of revenue instead of 57%.

Based on the people plan already defined, a reasonable Year-1 payroll baseline is about $302,975 across 5 roles in the plan.

This payroll estimate reflects the existing team plus any incremental additions from the staffing plan; it is not replacing the team already in place. That includes 1 current team role and 4 additional planned roles.

Does that broadly match your Year-1 payroll expectation, or should we adjust it because your actual payroll setup is materially different?
[user] Our Year-1 payroll will only include the owner, Emily Carter, with no additional hires initially. So the total payroll is $120,000 for her compensation. The $302,975 for multiple roles does not match our initial plan.

[financials][assistant] Thanks for clarifying — I’ll set Year-1 payroll to $120,000 for Emily only and remove the additional roles from the initial payroll. We’ll keep going from there.

A reasonable Year-1 marketing baseline is about 18% of revenue, which puts your projected Year-1 marketing spend around $396,396.

Does that broadly match what it will take to attract and convert customers in Year 1, or should we adjust it because your marketing spend will be materially different?
[user] Our marketing spend will be lower than that. We expect to spend about 10% of revenue on marketing in Year 1, so roughly $220,220, which should be sufficient given our online scheduling and paid ads approach.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll set your Year-1 marketing budget to about 10% of revenue (around $220k).

What do you pay each month for the space you use to run the business, like an office, storefront, clinic, kitchen, warehouse, or similar dedicated space?
[user] Our monthly rent expense is $9,500.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record your monthly rent as $9,500 per month.

Looking ahead, do you expect paid dedicated business space to stay part of how this business operates?
[user] Yes, paid dedicated business space will remain part of how the business operates.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll mark that you expect to keep paying for dedicated business space going forward.

As of last month, how much did you pay yourself from the business in wages, draws, or other owner compensation? A dollar amount is fine.
[user] I pay myself $10,000 per month, which totals $120,000 for the year as owner compensation.

[financials][assistant] Perfect, I’ll record your owner compensation as $120,000 per year.

As of last month, about how much did you spend on other regular business bills besides payroll, marketing, and rent, like utilities, software, insurance, accounting, phone, internet, and general overhead?
[user] Other operating expenses are about $4,000 per month, which covers utilities, software, insurance, accounting, phone, internet, and general overhead.

[financials][assistant] Got it, I’ll record your other operating expenses as about $4,000 per month.

As of last month, how many people were on payroll for the business, not counting outside contractors? A whole number is fine.
[user] There is only one person on the payroll, which is me as the owner.

[financials][assistant] Perfect, I’ll mark that as 1 person on payroll right now.

As of last month, did you make any larger one-time purchases for the business, like equipment, devices, furniture, build-out, or vehicles? If yes, what was the rough total?
[user] Yes, I made a larger one-time purchase recently totaling $60,000 for equipment and build-out.

[financials][assistant] Got it, I’ll record $60,000 as your recent one-time capital spend for equipment and build-out.

As of last month, what is your best rough estimate of the total value of the main equipment, devices, furniture, and fixtures already in the business?
[user] The total value of the main equipment, devices, furniture, and fixtures in the business is about $180,000.

[financials][assistant] Great, I’ll record your current equipment, furniture, and fixtures at about $180,000.

Now let's capture any leased or rented equipment or space beyond your main rent. What monthly amount should we use for any leased equipment, vehicles, servers, or additional space you do not own? If there is none, use 0.
[user] Use 2500 for monthly lease beyond main rent.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record $2,500 per month for leased items beyond your main rent.

As of last month, what is your best rough estimate of the total money or value put into the business so far by you or any investors?
[user] The total initial equity invested in the business is $50,000.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record $50,000 as the total initial equity invested so far.

As of last month, what was the total amount the business still owed on loans, lines of credit, or business credit cards?
[user] The total amount the business still owed on loans, lines of credit, or business credit cards is $120,000.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record $120,000 as the total debt outstanding.

As of last month, besides regular rent and credit card minimums already baked into other expenses, what other loan or debt payments did the business make each month?
[user] The business made other monthly debt payments of $1,500 last month besides regular rent and credit card minimums.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record $1,500 as your other monthly debt payments.

Of your debt payments, what is your best estimate of the annual interest cost, meaning the finance charge rather than principal paydown?
[user] The annual interest payment is about $9,000.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record your annual interest cost as about $9,000.

What is your best estimate of the annual principal you expect to repay on the business debt, separate from interest?
[user] The annual principal payment expected on the business debt is $18,000.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record $18,000 as your expected annual principal repayment on the business debt.

As of last month, about how much cash did the business have on hand in its bank accounts and any cash on site?
[user] As of last month, the business had about $15,000 in cash on hand.

[financials][assistant] Got it, I’ll record $15,000 as your cash on hand as of last month.

As of last month, about how much money did customers still owe you for completed work, like unpaid invoices or payment plans?
[user] Customers still owed about $2,000 for completed work as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record about $2,000 as your accounts receivable balance as of last month.

As of last month, about how much did the business still owe in regular operating bills, like unpaid supplier invoices, utilities, or business credit card balances related to operations?
[user] The business still owed about $12,000 in regular operating bills like unpaid supplier invoices and utilities as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Thanks—got it, I’ll record about $12,000 as your accounts payable balance as of last month.

As of last month, about how much inventory did you have on hand, like products or supplies kept in stock to use or sell?
[user] As of last month, the business had about $15,000 in inventory on hand.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record your inventory balance as about $15,000 as of last month.

One last financial planning question before I wrap this section up: when this business starts building extra cash, what would you want to do with it?

- Reinvest: Use extra cash to fund growth, capacity, or expansion when the economics support it.
- Preserve cash: Keep a thicker cash cushion and stay more conservative about putting excess cash back to work.
- Shareholder return: Treat excess cash as something that can be taken out of the business rather than just left to build up.
- Balanced: Keep a healthy cushion while still reinvesting selectively when it makes sense.

You can answer in plain language and I'll map it to the closest approach.
[user] I definitely want to reinvest extra cash back into the business to support hiring, expansion, and growth as the economics allow.

[done][assistant] Got it—I'll mark your cash strategy as reinvesting excess cash back into the business for growth.

Thanks. I have everything I need for financials, and the intake is complete.
